newsitem.title: JAPAN: Okinawa governor unlikely to back down on U.S. bases.
newsitem.headline: Okinawa governor unlikely to back down on U.S. bases.

text.p: Armed with a victory of sorts in a referendum on United States military bases, the governor of the southern Japan island of Okinawa travels to Tokyo on Tuesday to press his case with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

All signs indicate Governor Masahide Ota will not back down from his strong demands to reduce U.S. bases on his island, the subject of Sunday's referendum on Okinawa which saw an overwhelming 90 percent of the voters favour his approach.
Hashimoto said on Monday: "I would like to frankly accept the feelings of the 90 percent saying 'no' to the bases."

He told reporters: "We must continue with our efforts to consolidate and reduce the bases. But the bases will not be reduced to zero from 100 all at once," he said. "We would like them (Okinawans) to help with our efforts."

Ota, meanwhile, apparently unscathed by the relatively poor voter turnout of about 60 percent in the referendum, told a news conference late on Sunday: "We will continue to seek approval for the plan to close all U.S. bases by 2015."
Chief government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said on Monday that the government took the outcome of the referendum seriously and would continue to deal seriously with the problems faced by Okinawa.

On the meeting between Hashimoto and Ota, he told a news conference: "Prime Minister Hashimoto will deal with the Okinawa issue as one of the most important issues for the entire government. We hope the meeting will produce specific direction towards a solution of the issue."
Ota, playing down the turnout figure, said the U.S. bases are located in only half of Okinawa's 53 municipalities.
Okinawa is home to three-quarters of all U.S. military facilities in Japan, although it represents less than one percent of the country's total area.

The non-binding referendum did not mean the immediate closure of bases, nor did it settle the year-long confrontation between Okinawa and the central government, sparked by the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by U.S. servicemen last September.

But the vote, and a Supreme Court decision last month ruling against Ota's campaign to block the forced appropriation of land for U.S. bases, means the two sides will now be looking for a compromise solution.

Tokyo government sources said Hashimoto had dropped plans to use strong-arm tactics against Ota, namely a quick law that would enable the central government to bypass prefectural governments over land appropriation for U.S. bases.

Such a law would enable Hashimoto to smooth over land contracts, but would pose the danger of splitting the anti-bases Social Democratic Party, led by former premier Tomiichi Murayama, from his ruling coalition.
Sunday's vote also focused attention on the other part of an expected deal between Okinawa and the central government -- how to get Okinawa's economy out of its perennial doldrums.
Okinawa is the poorest of Japan's 47 prefectures, with a per capita income half that of Tokyo and an unemployment rate double the national average.
Ota said the low turnout showed there were strong fears that without the U.S. bases, the prefecture would go bankrupt.
"The 50 years the bases have been here have made them a structural part of the economy," Ota said. "We must do everything to remedy this situation."
For his part, Hashimoto played the humble role of an understanding chief of central government, saying the poll result was a "scolding" for not having done enough to lessen Okinawa's security burden.

Ota and Hashimoto now have to try to get what they want, or most likely a continued U.S. military presence in Okinawa for Tokyo and some face-saving streamlining of the bases for Ota plus a renewed plan to strengthen the island economy.

"With (Governor) Ota riding high after the plebiscite, he probably won't back down tomorrow (on Tuesday). But if he continues to resist, at some point the general Japanese public will think he's being unreasonable, or worse, grow tired of his cause," said John Neuffer, analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute.
"At that point, his battle is lost," he said.
Kajiyama said the U.S.-Japan security treaty was indispensable for Japan's security as well as peace and stability in Asia and the Pacific.
